extracted.intended_audience: readers of political economy (economists, policymakers, philanthropists, and the general educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and explaining the primary causes and mechanisms of recurring industrial depressions and the persistence of poverty amid advancing wealth in progressive societies, with special emphasis on land values and speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculative advance in land values as the main cause of industrial depressions
rubrics_metrics.description: The speculative advance in land values cuts down the earnings of labor and capital and checks production, and is the main cause of periodical industrial depressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduction and induction both indicate that speculation in land drives the phenomena of alternating activity and depression: rising land values force the margin of cultivation beyond its normal limit, compel labor and capital to accept smaller returns or to cease production, and thereby initiate widespread stoppages of production and demand. The author contrasts this with other theories and repeatedly returns to land speculation as the primary initiatory cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speculation must be in things of fixed quantity (land) to cause depressions
rubrics_metrics.description: If speculation is the cause of industrial depressions, it cannot be speculation in products of labor (which equalizes supply and demand); it must be speculation in things not produced by labor but necessary to it—i.e., land, a thing of fixed quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speculation in goods produced by labor tends to even out supply and demand; only speculation in fixed-quantity elements (land) can lock out labor and capital from productive use and produce the observed paralysis. This distinction is used to reject overproduction/overconsumption explanations that focus on speculation in commodities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism: speculative rent presses margin of cultivation and 'locks out' labor and capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculative advances in rent push the margin of cultivation beyond its normal limit so that labor and capital must accept smaller returns or cease production—effectively a lock-out of labor and capital by landowners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains that increasing land values appropriate returns that would otherwise go to labor and capital; where speculative prices exceed the returns possible under current production conditions, new increments of labor and capital cannot find employment at accustomed rates, leading to relative or absolute stoppage of production and propagated paralysis across industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagation through interdependence and credit: supply shocks become demand shocks
rubrics_metrics.description: A check to production in one sector propagates through the interlaced industrial system via exchanges and credit, turning a local production check into widespread cessation of demand and industrial paralysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because modern production is interdependent and exchanges are often made on credit, an initial check (often at the foundational land-based industries) reduces the supply of some commodities, which appears as a cessation of demand for others. The credit system's 'elastic' advances delay visible effects until a sudden 'snap' occurs, explaining the paroxysmal character of depressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other proximate contributory causes (not primary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Complexity and interdependence of production, defects of currencies, alternations in commercial credit, protective tariffs, and similar factors bear important part in producing and continuing hard times, but are proximate rather than primary causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author acknowledges these factors as significant contributors that affect propagation and severity, but insists they do not explain the initiatory cause the way land speculation does. These are treated as derivative forces that interact with the primary land-speculation cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Railroad construction and improvement anticipate land-value increases, fostering speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid extension of railroads is related to subsequent depression because railroad projects increase expectations of future land value, provoking land monopolization and speculative price increases that check production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wherever a railroad was built or projected, land values rose by speculation and were held at inflated prices; when the anticipated population/income increases did not immediately materialize, production was checked. The author cites California and transcontinental railroad expectations as clear illustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation for sudden 'paroxysms' of depression: delayed credit effects and elastic advances
rubrics_metrics.description: Although speculative pressure is progressive, depressions appear sudden because advances on credit from secondary industries to primary ones create an elastic connection that stretches and then breaks abruptly when foundational production is checked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the pyramid analogy: the lower ('primary') layer being contracted will not immediately show effect on upper layers due to credit and stock buffers; when the elastic connection fails it breaks 'with a snap', producing abrupt industrial crises (bank breaks, failures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions that restore equilibrium and end depressions
rubrics_metrics.description: A period of depression continues until one or more of the following occurs: (1) speculative land values are lost (fall); (2) increased efficiency of labor allows the normal rent line to overtake the speculative rent line; (3) labor and capital reconcile to engaging in production for smaller returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically all three factors co-operate to establish a new equilibrium and resume activity. The author also notes that after each cycle wages and interest are gradually forced toward a lower minimum overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of poverty amid advancing wealth: increasing productive power raises rent, depressing wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Although civilization increases productive power and could extirpate poverty, the benefits are intercepted by owners of land: every increase in productive power increases rent, which forces wages toward a subsistence minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues that land being necessary to production and privately owned causes the gains of progress to accrue to landowners rather than labor; thus increases in productive power do not raise wages proportionately because higher earnings are extracted as rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of overproduction/overconsumption explanations as complete accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories that attribute depressions solely to overproduction or overconsumption are inadequate: masses want more wealth and are willing to produce it, so the real issue is that production and consumption cannot meet because labor is denied access to land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author uses common-sense examples (warehouses full while people want goods) to show that the problem is not want but inability to produce because of access barriers to land; overproduction/overconsumption describe symptoms but not the underlying cause (land speculation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly of land and speculative holding prevents labor employing itself on unused land
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in regions with unused land, labor cannot employ itself there because land has been monopolized and held at speculative prices based on anticipated future population and values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: San Francisco—nearby unused land exists but is held at speculative prices; hence unemployed urban labor cannot turn to land employment. The text emphasizes that access to land, not sheer land availability, is the constraint.
